text.tspan: The residual connection: the input x is added straight back. Because of this, attention only has to supply a CORRECTION to
each word, never rebuild it — and the gradient gets a path back to the embeddings that skips attention entirely, which is what
keeps deep stacks trainable. Section C measures the two vectors being added. For "dog" in sequence A, x has length

the same pattern with three sub-layers instead of two.

text.tspan: Everything above runs twice: each layer takes the previous layer’s output, so the second layer runs attention over a sentence
that has already been rewritten once. After the last layer this tensor is
— the only thing the decoder ever sees of the
source sentence, read through cross-attention in
. It is computed once per batch, even when
is two statistics and a division

sounds technical, but it is only three steps on one row of numbers: find their mean, subtract it, and divide by their standard deviation. Both statistics come from the row itself, so nothing about the other sentence, the other words or the batch size can affect the result.

Why the addition comes before the normalisation
At this untrained stage the input is only about
across the batch), so each sum is a real mix of the word and a still-random correction, which
then rescales. Two layers train fine this way. In a very deep post-norm stack, though, every one of those rescalings sits on
the main path the gradient has to travel back through, which is why such models need a careful learning-rate warm-up to train at all.
